User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to tr

eat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: I can help — below is a practical, clear breakdown of what you can likely deduct, whether itemizing makes sense, how to treat the home office, what tax forms you’ll use, and what I need from you to tighten the estimates.

Summary (quick)
- Income to report: W-2 $68,200; self-employment (photography) $16,300 (Schedule C); interest income $2,520 (likely Form 1099‑INT / Schedule B).
- Likely best to take the standard deduction (single) for 2024 — your item

izable deductions shown ($1,500 charity) are well below the standard deduction.
- Business deductions (photography) and the home-office deduction lower your taxable/self‑employment income regardless of itemizing.
- Student loan interest: only interest paid in the tax year (2024) is deductible and the maximum allowable deduction is $2,500 (phaseouts apply). If you paid $5,100 across multiple years, only 2024 payments count.
- You’ll need Form 1040, Schedule C, Schedule SE, Schedule 1 (for student loan intere

st and half SE tax deduction), Schedule B (because interest > $1,500), plus any 1099s and Form 1098‑E if available.

Key details and calculations (estimates)
Assumptions used below:
- Your $2,100 (Capital One 360) and $420 (Merrill Edge) are interest income.
- The $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” are business expenses for your photography work (if they are unreimbursed employee expenses for your W‑2 job, they are NOT deductible on federal returns).
- Student loan interest deduction assumes you actually paid t

hat interest in 2024 (see questions below).
- Rent $1,750/month → $21,000/year.

Totals before deductions:
- W-2 wages: $68,200
- Photography income (gross): $16,300
- Interest income: $2,520
Total gross income = $87,020

Home-office — two methods
You have a 120 sq ft exclusive office in a 740 sq ft rental (exclusive use claimed). Office share = 120/740 ≈ 16.216%.

A) Simplified method:
- Allowed: $5 per sq ft up to 300 sq ft → 120 * $5 = $600 deduction.
B) Actual expense method (usually yields larger deduc

tion here):
- Rent portion for office = 16.216% × $21,000 = $3,405.
- (You could also include a share of utilities, renter’s insurance, internet if you pay them — you didn’t list amounts.)

Effect on your self‑employment income (examples)

1) Using the simplified home‑office method:
- Gross photography: $16,300
- Less business expenses (assume $1,050) and home office $600
- Net profit = $16,300 − $1,050 − $600 = $14,650
- SE tax (approx): net × 92.35% × 15.3% ≈ $2,070
- Half SE tax deductible (adjustment to

income) ≈ $1,035

2) Using the actual home‑office allocation:
- Net profit = $16,300 − $1,050 − $3,405 = $11,845
- SE tax ≈ $1,674
- Half SE tax deductible ≈ $837

How these interact with other deductions:
- Student loan interest: up to $2,500 above‑the‑line deduction (on Schedule 1), subject to income phaseout rules — this reduces your AGI whether or not you itemize.
- Charitable $1,500: only deductible if you itemize (Schedule A).
- Standard deduction (single) for 2024 is about $14,600. With only $1,500

in charitable donations and no other itemized items listed (mortgage interest, big state taxes, large medical expenses, etc.), you will very likely take the standard deduction.

Rough taxable-income illustration (rounded, simplified):
- Using actual home office (the more favorable case above) and assuming you can claim $2,500 student loan interest:
  - AGI approximation after adjustments ≈ (W-2 68,200 + net business 11,845 + interest 2,520) − half SE tax 837 − student loan interest 2,500 ≈ $79,200
  - Minus

standard deduction ~$14,600 → taxable income ≈ $64,600
- If you used the simplified method taxable income would be a bit higher. These are illustrative — final numbers will vary with exact figures and any additional deductions/credits.

Other important items and possible tax consequences
- Self‑employment tax: you’ll owe SE tax on net self‑employment earnings (we estimated it above). Half of that SE tax is an adjustment to income.
- Estimated tax/withholding: because of SE tax and additional income, you ma

y need quarterly estimated payments unless you increase withholding on your W‑2 to cover the gap.
- QBI (20% Qualified Business Income deduction): you may be eligible for up to 20% of qualified business income — this is a complex calculation but could further reduce taxable income. It’s worth checking when you prepare the return.
- Keep receipts and good records: invoices, 1099s, bank statements, donation receipts, lease/rent records, bills for utilities, and documentation showing exclusive use of the home

office (sketch of space and size).

Forms you’ll likely need
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1 (adjustments like student loan interest and deduction for half of SE tax)
- Schedule C (Profit or Loss from Business) — to report photography income and business expenses, including the home-office expense
- Schedule SE — for self‑employment tax
- Schedule B — if total interest/dividends > $1,500 (you have $2,520 interest)
- Form 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC (if you received these from clients) — attach/report amounts on Schedule C

- Form 1098‑E — student loan interest statement (if you have one) to support the student loan interest deduction
- Schedule A — only if you end up itemizing (unlikely with numbers shown)
- Form 8995/8995‑A — if claiming QBI deduction (software/tax pro may file this)

Questions I need to give you a precise answer / next steps
1. Did you actually pay $5,100 in student loan interest in 2024, or is that the total paid across multiple years (2018–2021 etc.)? Only interest paid in 2024 is deductible now. Do you h

ave Form 1098‑E for 2024?
2. Are the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” business expenses for the photography work (equipment, travel, supplies, etc.), or are they unreimbursed employee expenses for your W‑2 job? If they’re employee unreimbursed expenses, they’re not deductible for federal purposes.
3. Does your rent payment ($1,750) include utilities and internet, or are those billed separately? (If separate, tell me amounts for possible larger actual home office deduction.)
4. Did you receive any 1099‑NEC/109

9‑MISC from your photography clients? If so, how many and amounts by payer?
5. Do you want me to do a tighter numeric estimate of your federal tax (including SE tax and possible quarterly payment amount) using the choices above (simplified vs actual home office and student loan interest amount)?

Recommendation
- If you want the largest home‑office deduction and you have good records, use the actual allocation method (it appears larger here).
- You will almost certainly take the standard deduction unless yo

u have significant other itemizable deductions (property tax, mortgage interest, large medical expenses).
- Make sure you have Form 1098‑E for student loan interest and any 1099s. Keep receipts for donations and business expenses.
- Consider making estimated tax payments (or increasing W‑2 withholding) to cover SE tax and income tax on the photography income.

If you want, I can:
- Run a full, line‑by‑line estimate of your 2024 federal tax (I’ll need answers to the 5 clarifying questions above).
- Produce a

checklist of documents to gather for filing.
- Draft an email template for your accountant (if you want to forward this summary).

Which would you like next?
